lines.text: Three meters of timber, and one line down its whole length. No straightedge that long, no pencil. Just a string, and a snap.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Every kind of line on a timber has its own tool. This episode, we meet them.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The string comes from a sumitsubo, the carpenter's ink line. At the front is a small pond, the ike, packed with silk floss soaked in ink. Behind it, a reel holds the line. At the line's end is a pin, the karuko. Traditional pots were carved from mulberry; zelkova is common today.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Push the pin into one end of the mark. Draw the line out through the inked floss, and pull it taut to the other end.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Lift it straight up, and let it go. The line slaps down and leaves a straight ink line, even across a slightly uneven surface.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: A Western chalk line works the same way. The difference is what's left behind: chalk wipes off easily. Ink pots come in sizes from about eighteen to thirty centimeters long; the biggest were for temple and shrine work.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: For everything shorter, there's the sumisashi, the ink pen. It's a strip of bamboo, flattened. One end is cut on a slant and split into fine slits, so it holds ink and draws a clean line.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The other end is rounded and crushed into a little brush, for writing marks and words. The notes on the story stick in the first episode were written this way.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Now, the promise from last time: how to square a line with a flat steel square that has no thick stock.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: One arm hooks over the edge of the board. Its inner edge presses against the side, held by your fingers near the middle of that arm. The other arm lies across the face, and you draw along it.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Simply laying the square on top of the board doesn't work: nothing holds it square to the edge. That's why the edge you hook must be straight and true: it's the reference face. And which arm hooks the edge varies; you'll see both.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: For lines parallel to an edge, there's the kebiki, the marking gauge. A fence slides along a planed edge, and a small blade at the end of the beam scores a line. Set the distance once, and the gauge repeats it on every piece, just as the story stick repeats lengths.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: For lines parallel to an edge, there's the keh-bee-kee, the marking gauge. A fence slides along a planed edge, and a small blade at the end of the beam scores a line. Set the distance once, and the gauge repeats it on every piece, just as the story stick repeats lengths.

lines.text: Because it cuts with a blade, it's closest to a Western cutting gauge, not a pin gauge. A pin tends to tear the fibers across the grain. A blade slices them.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: There are many kinds. The sujikebiki just scores lines. The warikebiki cuts deeper, to split thin boards to width.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: There are many kinds. The soo-jee-keh-bee-kee just scores lines. The wah-ree-keh-bee-kee cuts deeper, to split thin boards to width.

lines.text: And for the finest lines, a marking knife: the shiragaki, also called shirabiki. Most are flat on the back and beveled on one side.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: A knife line is a fine cut, not just a mark on the surface. When and how to use one comes with the cutting tools.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Next time, we go back to the board plan, and follow the lines from the plan onto the timber.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Snap the long lines. Write with the pen. Square with the sashigane, gauge the parallels, and knife the finest. Every line has its tool.
